title: Distributed Transactions
subtitle: Atomic commitment across shards and services: Two-Phase Commit (2PC), coordinator blocking bottlenecks, and Google Percolator / Spanner.
keyTakeaways: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) achieves atomic all-or-nothing commits across multiple database shards using a Prepare (Voting) phase and a Commit phase.

2PC is a **blocking protocol**: if a participant votes `YES` in Phase 1 and the Coordinator crashes before broadcasting Phase 2, the participant cannot unilaterally abort or commit—holding locks indefinitely.

Modern Distributed SQL databases (Google Spanner, CockroachDB) combine 2PC across shards with Raft/Paxos consensus groups inside each shard soneither the coordinator nor participants are single points of failure.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Distributed Transactions is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Atomic commitment across shards and services: Two-Phase Commit (2PC), coordinator blocking bottlenecks, and Google Percolator / Spanner. Fundamentally, When a single transaction must atomically update data living on two separate physical shards (or two separate databases via XA), a Transaction Coordinator orchestrates Two-Phase Commit (2PC). In **Phase 1 (Prepare)**, the coordinator asks all participants if they *can* commit. Voting `YES` is a binding promise: the participant must acquire all locks, validate constraints, and flush its redo/undo log records to disk before replying `YES`. In **Phase 2 (Commit/Abort)**, if all participants voted `YES`, the coordinator writes a commit decision to its own WAL and tells all participants to commit; if any voted `NO` or timed out, it tells all to roll back.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) achieves atomic all-or-nothing commits across multiple database shards using a Prepare (Voting) phase and a Commit phase.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: 2PC is a **blocking protocol**: if a participant votes `YES` in Phase 1 and the Coordinator crashes before broadcasting Phase 2, the participant cannot unilaterally abort or commit—holding locks indefinitely.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, distributed transactions manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **Two-Phase Commit (2PC / XA / Distributed SQL)**: Focuses on provides strict acid atomicity and serializability across multiple shards; no compensating logic needed. Best suited for Cross-shard financial transfers within the same Distributed SQL database (Spanner/CockroachDB)..

**Asynchronous Saga Pattern (Compensating Transactions)**: Focuses on no distributed locks held across network calls; decouples availability of independent microservices. Best suited for Cross-microservice workflows spanning heterogeneous databases or external third-party APIs..

Why Participants Cannot Back Out After Voting YES: Once a participant replies `YES`, it enters an 'in-doubt' state. If the Coordinator crashes right after collecting votes, the participant doesn't know whether the other shard already received `GLOBAL_COMMIT`. It must hold its row locks and wait until the Coordinator recovers!
Latency Multiplication: 2PC requires multiple synchronous network round-trips and multiple sequential disk `fsync` barriers across all participating nodes, amplifying lock hold duration by 5–10x.

High-Availability Coordinator: Both the Coordinator and every Participant shard are replicated across 3–5 nodes via Raft/Paxos. If one physical machine crashes during Phase 1, the Raft group elects a new leader in milliseconds and completes the 2PC without blocking!

Google Percolator / Parallel Commits: CockroachDB pipelines the Coordinator commit record and Participant intent staging in parallel, cutting distributed commit latency to a single consensus round-trip.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around distributed transactions unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Cross-shard financial transfers within the same Distributed SQL database (Spanner/CockroachDB). and environments requiring Provides strict ACID atomicity and serializability across multiple shards; no compensating logic needed..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Cross-microservice workflows spanning heterogeneous databases or external third-party APIs. where No distributed locks held across network calls; decouples availability of independent microservices..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: If 2PC is slow and fragile when a single Coordinator machine crashes, how do Google Spanner and CockroachDB run distributed ACID transactions at massive scale? Instead of running 2PC across fragile single machines, they run **2PC across Raft/Paxos Consensus Groups**.. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, distributed transactions introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose holds locks across network round-trips; couples availability of all participating shards.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when lacks isolation (intermediate state is visible); requires writing idempotent compensating actions.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering distributed transactions is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Modern Distributed SQL databases (Google Spanner, CockroachDB) combine 2PC across shards with Raft/Paxos consensus groups inside each shard soneither the coordinator nor participants are single points of failure.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: In a microservice architecture where Order Service, Payment Service, and Inventory Service each own private databases, advise *against* XA / 2PC across services (because holding DB locks over HTTP/RPC kills availability) and propose the Saga Pattern instead.
